message.content:
{"passages":[{"reference":"12.6","text":"When Peter heard this, he said jokingly, “What then do you think, Clement? Do you suppose that by sheer necessity you are to be assigned a place among my servants? For who will look after the many fine linen garments, together with the rings and footwear that accompany me? And who will prepare the pleasant and costly foods, which, being varied, require many skilled cooks—and all those things that, procured through every kind of greed, are prepared for the desire of effeminate people as though for a huge wild beast? But if a resolve has crept into you in this way, perhaps it is because you did not understand and did not know my way of life: I subsist on bread alone and olives, and only rarely on vegetables. The garment I have—a worn cloak—is this very one I am wearing, and I have no need of another or of anything else; indeed, in these things I have more than enough. For my mind, seeing all the eternal good things there, does not look around at any of the things here.

“Nevertheless, I welcome your good resolve, and with admiration I praise how readily you, a man accustomed to luxurious habits, have changed your way of life to one of mere necessities. For from childhood we—I and Andrew, who is my brother both by blood and according to God—were not only brought up as orphans but were also accustomed by poverty and hardship to a life of labor. We therefore now bear the hardships of the roads with ease. Consequently, if you listened to me, you would permit me, a working man, to perform a servant’s duties for you.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"μὴ ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ἀνάγκης σε εἰς δούλων μοι ταγῆναι τόπον;","chosen":"Do you suppose that by sheer necessity you are to be assigned a place among my servants?","rationale":"The μή-question is an incredulous, joking question. “Servants” follows the supplied wording policy for δοῦλος, while the underlying term can denote enslaved household members."},{"source_quote":"τὰς καλὰς καὶ πολλὰς σινδόνας","chosen":"the many fine linen garments","rationale":"σινδόνες can denote fine linen cloths or garments. The surrounding references to personal rings and footwear favor garments, though “fine linen cloths” remains possible."},{"source_quote":"μετὰ τῶν ἐπομένων μοι δακτυλίων καὶ ὑποδήσεων","chosen":"together with the rings and footwear that accompany me","rationale":"The dative μοι identifies Peter as the person whom the rings and footwear accompany or with whom they are associated; it does not make them accessories belonging to the linen garments."},{"source_quote":"ὅσα ἐκτεθηλυμμένων ἀνθρώπων ὡς θηρίῳ μεγάλῳ τῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐκ πάσης πλεονεξίας πορισθέντα ἑτοιμάζεται","chosen":"all those things that, procured through every kind of greed, are prepared for the desire of effeminate people as though for a huge wild beast","rationale":"The rendering retains the author’s disparaging description, the comparison of desire to a large wild beast, and the charge that these things are acquired through greed."},{"source_quote":"ἱμάτιόν μοι καὶ τριβώνιον ὑπάρχει τοῦτ’ αὐτὸ ὃ περιβέβλημαι","chosen":"The garment I have—a worn cloak—is this very one I am wearing","rationale":"τριβώνιον denotes a worn or rough cloak. The nouns are read appositionally, emphasizing that Peter possesses only the garment currently around him; alternatively, the wording could be represented more formally as “my garment and cloak are this very thing I am wearing.”"},{"source_quote":"ἐν γὰρ τούτοις καὶ περισσεύομαι","chosen":"indeed, in these things I have more than enough","rationale":"περισσεύομαι conveys abundance or surplus rather than mere adequacy."},{"source_quote":"Ἀνδρέας ὁ σύναιμος καὶ κατὰ θεὸν ἀδελφὸς ὢν ἐμός","chosen":"Andrew, who is my brother both by blood and according to God","rationale":"The literal expression “according to God” is retained rather than reduced to the interpretive label “spiritual brother.”"},{"source_quote":"τὰς τῶν ὁδῶν φέρομεν σκύλσεις","chosen":"we bear the hardships of the roads","rationale":"σκύλσεις can denote vexations, harassment, or hardships. “Hardships” suits the rigors of travel without restricting the expression to one kind of difficulty."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"πλὴν εἰ τοιαύτῃ σε προαίρεσις ὑπεισῆλθεν","issue":"The printed τοιαύτῃ is dative although προαίρεσις is nominative. The main translation provisionally understands τοιαύτῃ adverbially, “in this way.” A conjectural nominative τοιαύτη would instead give the more regular construction “if such a resolve has crept into you.” The image-checked printed reading has not been altered.","proposed_reading":"πλὴν εἰ τοιαύτη σε προαίρεσις ὑπεισῆλθεν","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"12.7","text":"When I heard this, I began trembling and became tearful at such a statement from a man to whom all the people of the present generation are inferior in the matter of knowledge and piety. When he saw me in tears, he asked the reason for my tears. I said, “What wrong have I committed that you should say such a thing to me?”

Peter answered, “If it was wrong of me to speak of serving you, you were the first to do wrong, since you thought it proper to do this for me.”

I said, “It is not the same. It is entirely fitting for me to do this, but for you, the herald of God who saves our souls, it is a grievous thing to do this for me.”

Peter answered, “I would agree with you, except that our Lord, who came for the salvation of the whole world and who alone was noble above everyone, endured servitude so that he might persuade us not to be ashamed to perform servants’ services for our brothers, even if we happen to be exceedingly noble.”

I said, “If I think I can defeat you in argument, I am foolish. Nevertheless, I give thanks to God’s providence that I was deemed worthy to have you in the place of parents.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"οἷον λόγον εἶπεν ἀνήρ, οὗ πάντες οἱ τῆς νῦν γενεᾶς ἄνθρωποι τῷ τῆς γνώσεως καὶ εὐσεβείας λόγῳ ἥττους τυγχάνουσιν","chosen":"at such a statement from a man to whom all the people of the present generation are inferior in the matter of knowledge and piety","rationale":"οἷον gives the statement an emphatic quality. The second λόγῳ is taken as indicating the respect or matter in which the present generation is inferior rather than as naming a separate discourse."},{"source_quote":"τὸ δουλεῦσαί σοι","chosen":"serving you","rationale":"The infinitive denotes performing a subordinate or servile role for Clement. “Serving” is natural here, while the stronger status nuance of the cognate δουλεία is represented by “servitude” later in the passage."},{"source_quote":"τοῦτ᾿ ἐμοὶ ποιῆσαι ἀξιώσας","chosen":"since you thought it proper to do this for me","rationale":"The infinitive is understood with Clement as its subject: he had considered it fitting to perform such service for Peter. A more formal rendering would be “having deemed it worthy to do this for me.”"},{"source_quote":"Συνεθέμην ἂν σοι, ἐπεὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν","chosen":"I would agree with you, except that our Lord","rationale":"The unreal “I would agree” is followed by the consideration that prevents agreement. Although ἐπεί commonly means “since,” its contextual force here can be expressed as “except that” or “were it not that.”"},{"source_quote":"μόνος ὑπὲρ πάντας εὐγενὴς ὢν","chosen":"who alone was noble above everyone","rationale":"εὐγενής can mean noble or well-born. The wording preserves the comparison with all others without specifying whether the author’s emphasis is social birth, inherent nobility, or both."},{"source_quote":"δουλείαν ὑπέμεινεν","chosen":"endured servitude","rationale":"δουλεία denotes the condition or service of a servant or slave. “Servitude” preserves the stronger status nuance without specifying an episode not named by the source."},{"source_quote":"εἰς γονέων τόπον","chosen":"in the place of parents","rationale":"The plural γονέων is retained: Clement regards Peter as occupying the place held collectively by his parents."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.8","text":"Peter asked, “Do you truly have no one related to you by birth?”

I answered, “There are indeed many prominent men of Caesar’s family. That is why Caesar himself, since my father had also been brought up with him, arranged for a female relative to be joined in marriage to my father. From her we were born, three sons: two before me, who were twins and were extremely like each other, as my father himself used to tell me. For I do not remember either them or the woman who bore me very well, but, as though through dreams, I call up a dim image of them.

“My mother, then, was called Mattidia, and my father Faustus. As for my brothers themselves, one was called Faustinus and the other Faustinianus. After I was born to them as their third child, my mother saw a dream—as my father used to recount—that unless she immediately took her twin sons and left the city of the Romans to live abroad for ten years, she was destined to die together with them by an utterly ruinous fate.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Οὐδεὶς δέ σου ἀληθῶς πρὸς γένος ὑπάρχει;","chosen":"Do you truly have no one related to you by birth?","rationale":"πρὸς γένος asks about kinship or family connection. “By birth” distinguishes this relationship from Peter’s preceding reference to brotherhood “according to God.”"},{"source_quote":"Εἰσὶν μὲν πολλοὶ καὶ μεγάλοι ἄνδρες, Καίσαρος πρὸς γένους ὄντες","chosen":"There are indeed many prominent men of Caesar’s family","rationale":"μεγάλοι describes the men as great or prominent, while Καίσαρος πρὸς γένους indicates family or kinship connection with Caesar."},{"source_quote":"ὡς καὶ συντρόφῳ","chosen":"since my father had also been brought up with him","rationale":"σύντροφος can denote a childhood companion, foster-brother, or someone reared together with another. The rendering preserves shared upbringing without asserting formal fosterage."},{"source_quote":"ἐγὼ γὰρ οὔτε αὐτοὺς. οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν πάνυ ἐπίσταμαι","chosen":"For I do not remember either them or the woman who bore me very well","rationale":"ἐπίσταμαι ordinarily means “know,” but the following reference to a dim mental image makes recollection the contextual sense. With the negation, πάνυ is represented as “very well.”"},{"source_quote":"ὥσπερ δι᾿ ὀνείρων ἀμαυρὸν αὐτῶν τὸ εἶδος ἀναφέρω","chosen":"as though through dreams, I call up a dim image of them","rationale":"ἀναφέρω here concerns bringing an image back to mind. The translation retains both the dreamlike comparison and the indistinctness of the remembered appearance."},{"source_quote":"ἐξαυτῆς παραλαβοῦσα","chosen":"unless she immediately took","rationale":"ἐξαυτῆς means “immediately” or “at once,” not “by herself.”"},{"source_quote":"πανολεθρίῳ μόρῳ ἅμα αὐτοῖς ἀποθανεῖν ἔχει","chosen":"she was destined to die together with them by an utterly ruinous fate","rationale":"πανολέθριος conveys complete ruin or destruction, μόρος can mean doom, fate, or death, and ἀποθανεῖν ἔχει expresses an impending or destined death. “By an utterly ruinous fate” preserves the source’s separate reference to doom without repeating “death” in English."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἐγὼ γὰρ οὔτε αὐτοὺς. οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν πάνυ ἐπίσταμαι","issue":"The printed period interrupts the correlative construction οὔτε … οὔτε. The translation treats the clauses as grammatically continuous while preserving all the printed words. This appears to be an editorial punctuation oddity rather than missing content.","proposed_reading":"ἐγὼ γὰρ οὔτε αὐτοὺς οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν πάνυ ἐπίσταμαι","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"12.9","text":"Our father, then, being devoted to his children, adequately supplied them for the journey with male and female servants, put them aboard a ship, and sent them away to Athens so that the boys would be educated together. But he kept only me, his son, with him as consolation. For this I give abundant thanks: that the dream had not commanded me too to leave the city of the Romans with my mother.

“When a year had passed, my father sent money to Athens for his own people and at the same time sent to learn how they were doing. But those who went did not return. In the third year my father, becoming despondent, likewise sent others with provisions. They came in the fourth year and reported that they had seen neither my mother nor my brothers, that the missing family had not even been in Athens itself, and that they had not found so much as a trace of anyone else who had gone away with them.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"φιλότεκνος ὢν","chosen":"being devoted to his children","rationale":"φιλότεκνος describes strong affection for one’s children. “Devoted” suits both the father’s preparations and his subsequent search."},{"source_quote":"σύν τε δούλοις καὶ δούλαις","chosen":"with male and female servants","rationale":"Both the masculine and feminine forms are represented. In this household context they may denote enslaved attendants; “servants” follows the supplied wording policy while the possible bonded status remains disclosed."},{"source_quote":"εἰς τὰς Ἀθήνας ἅμα παιδευθησομένους ἐξέπεμψεν","chosen":"sent them away to Athens so that the boys would be educated together","rationale":"The masculine plural παιδευθησομένους most naturally refers to the twin sons rather than to their mother. ἅμα is taken as “together,” though “at the same time” is lexically possible."},{"source_quote":"ἐμὲ δὲ μόνον υἱὸν εἰς παραμυθίαν ἔσχεν μεθ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ","chosen":"he kept only me, his son, with him as consolation","rationale":"εἰς παραμυθίαν identifies Clement as a source of comfort or consolation after the others’ departure."},{"source_quote":"χρήματα τοῖς αὐτοῦ ἅμα τε καὶ μαθεῖν τὸ πῶς διάγουσιν","chosen":"sent money to Athens for his own people and at the same time sent to learn how they were doing","rationale":"τοῖς αὐτοῦ means “for his own people,” contextually the absent family. The agents sent to make inquiries are left implicit in this clause and become explicit in οἱ δὲ ἀπελθόντες, “those who went.”"},{"source_quote":"μήτε μὴν αὐταῖς Ἀθήναις ἐπιδεδημηκέναι","chosen":"that the missing family had not even been in Athens itself","rationale":"Here the unexpressed subject is taken as Clement’s mother and brothers, because the searchers were sent to Athens and their report concerns the missing family. Alternatively, the continuing subject may be the searchers, reporting that they had not stayed or resided in Athens itself. The Greek does not explicitly mark a change of subject."},{"source_quote":"κἂν ἴχνος εὑρηκέναι","chosen":"that they had not found so much as a trace","rationale":"κἄν strengthens the negation: the searchers found not even a trace."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.10","text":"When my father heard these things, he became bewildered by his great grief. Not knowing where he should set out to search for them, he took me with him, went down to Portus, and repeatedly questioned many people about where each one had seen or heard of a shipwreck that had occurred four years earlier. One person named one place, another a different place. He in turn asked whether they had seen the body of a woman with young children washed ashore. . When those people said that they had seen many corpses in many places, my father groaned on hearing it. Yet, because his inward affections were in turmoil, he kept making irrational inquiries, since he was attempting to search so vast an expanse of sea. Still, he could be excused, because through his affection for those being sought he was being fed on empty hopes.

“And so, eventually, he placed me under guardians and left me in Rome when I was twelve years old. Then he himself went down to Portus in tears, boarded a ship, put out to sea, and departed on the search. From that time until this very day I have neither received any letters from him nor learned with certainty whether he is alive or dead. Rather, I suspect that he too has died somewhere, either overcome by grief or overtaken by shipwreck. The evidence for this is that it is now the twentieth year since then, and since that time I have heard no reliable news at all about him.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"εἰς Πόρτον","chosen":"to Portus","rationale":"Πόρτος is treated as the proper name of Rome’s harbor rather than translated generically as “the port.”"},{"source_quote":"ἀπὸ τεσσάρων ἐτῶν γενόμενον ναυφράγιον","chosen":"a shipwreck that had occurred four years earlier","rationale":"The phrase can designate a wreck from four years before the inquiry. A broader contextual alternative is “a shipwreck during the preceding four years.”"},{"source_quote":"σῶμα γυναικὸς μετὰ βρεφῶν ἐκβεβρασμένον","chosen":"the body of a woman with young children washed ashore","rationale":"βρέφη can denote infants or very young children. “Young children” avoids fixing their precise age, while ἐκβεβρασμένον depicts the woman’s body as cast or washed ashore."},{"source_quote":"τῶν οὖν πολλὰ λεγόντων ἑωρακέναι πτώματα κατὰ πολλοὺς τόπους","chosen":"When those people said that they had seen many corpses in many places","rationale":"The neuter accusative plural πολλὰ is taken with the neuter accusative plural πτώματα, supported by their agreement and the parallel πολλοὺς τόπους. Alternatively, πολλὰ may attach adverbially to λεγόντων: “when those who spoke at length said that they had seen corpses in many places.”"},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ σπλάγχνων θορυβούμενος","chosen":"because his inward affections were in turmoil","rationale":"σπλάγχνα literally denotes inward organs and figuratively deep affections. “Inward affections” retains more of the source image than a purely abstract reference to emotion."},{"source_quote":"τοσοῦτον μέγεθος θαλάττης ἐρευνᾶν","chosen":"to search so vast an expanse of sea","rationale":"The expression emphasizes the immense extent of sea that he was irrationally attempting to investigate."},{"source_quote":"τῇ πρὸς τοὺς ζητουμένους στοργῇ ἐλπίσιν ἐβουκολεῖτο κεναῖς","chosen":"through his affection for those being sought he was being fed on empty hopes","rationale":"βουκολέω literally evokes feeding or tending a herd and can figuratively mean sustaining or beguiling someone with expectations. The main rendering preserves the feeding image; “he was beguiled by empty hopes” is a less image-retentive alternative."},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ φροντιστὰς ποιήσας με","chosen":"he placed me under guardians","rationale":"φροντισταί are people charged with oversight or care. “Guardians” suits the care of a twelve-year-old, though “caretakers” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"ἤδη λοιπὸν ἔκτοτε εἰκοστὸν ἔτος ἐστίν","chosen":"it is now the twentieth year since then","rationale":"The ordinal expression is retained rather than converted into an exact modern elapsed-year count."},{"source_quote":"ἀφ’ ἧς οὐδεμίαν τινὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ ἀλήθειαν ἤκουσα","chosen":"since that time I have heard no reliable news at all about him","rationale":"ἀφ’ ἧς is understood elliptically as “since that time” or “since that day,” extending the absence of information from the father’s departure to the present. ἀλήθεια here denotes true or dependable information rather than abstract truth."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἐκβεβρασμένον. .","issue":"The image-checked edition prints two dots separated by a space after ἐκβεβρασμένον. Their function remains uncertain: they may mark unavailable wording or may be an editorial punctuation oddity. The English retains exactly “. .” at this point and supplies no restoration. If the dots mark a lacuna, its content is unavailable.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"εἰς πλοῖον ἐνβάς","issue":"The edition prints the unassimilated spelling ἐνβάς. It is intelligible as the participle ordinarily normalized as ἐμβάς, “having boarded.” The printed form is verified and no missing wording is involved.","proposed_reading":"εἰς πλοῖον ἐμβάς","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
